rules.title: When?
rules.text: Things that happen **again and again** – or **never**.
rules.textDe: Was immer wieder oder nie passiert.

rules.title: he / she / it → -s
rules.text: Watch the spelling: go → **goes**, watch → **watches**, try → **tries**.
rules.textDe: Achte auf die Schreibung.

rules.title: Not
rules.text: **don't / doesn't** + base form
rules.textDe: don't/doesn't + Grundform

rules.title: Questions
rules.text: **Do / Does** + base form? Short answer: Yes, I **do**. / No, he **doesn't**.
rules.textDe: Frage mit Do/Does, Kurzantwort mit do/does.

rules.title: Question words
rules.text: Question word + **do / does** + base form
rules.textDe: Fragewort + do/does + Grundform

rules.title: Signal words
rules.text: always · usually · often · sometimes · never · every day · on Mondays
rules.textDe: Diese Wörter zeigen: simple present!

challenge.title: Challenge: Who?
challenge.text: Who asks for the **subject** (wer?): no do/does → **Who likes** Ben? · Who asks for the **object** (wen?): with do/does → **Who does** Ben like?

camp.title: Start: we read the rules together
camp.text: We started our trip, did the check-in and read the **rules** of the simple present together.
camp.textDe: Wir haben die Reise gestartet, den Check-in gemacht und die Regeln des simple present gemeinsam gelesen.

rules.title: When?
rules.text: Finished actions at a **time in the past**: yesterday · last summer · two days ago · in 2016
rules.textDe: Was abgeschlossen ist und zu einem Zeitpunkt in der Vergangenheit passiert ist.

rules.title: Regular verbs → -ed
rules.text: Watch the spelling: stop → **stopped**, try → **tried**, love → **loved**.
rules.textDe: Achte auf die Schreibung.

rules.title: Irregular verbs
rules.text: Learn them: go → **went**, see → **saw**, swim → **swam**, eat → **ate**, take → **took**.
rules.textDe: Eigene Form – lernen!
rules.ex: I **saw** a turtle. It **swam** under me.

rules.title: was / were
rules.text: I / he / she / it → **was** · you / we / they → **were** · not: **wasn't / weren't**
rules.textDe: be hat zwei Formen – ohne did.

rules.title: Not
rules.text: **didn't** + base form
rules.textDe: didn't + Grundform

rules.title: Questions
rules.text: **Did** + subject + base form? Short answer: Yes, I **did**. / No, I **didn't**. With be: **Were** you …? – Yes, I **was**.
rules.textDe: Frage mit Did + Grundform; bei be mit Was/Were.

challenge.title: Challenge: Who?
challenge.text: Who asks for the **subject** (wer?): no did → **Who saw** the turtle? · Who asks for the **object** (wen?): with did → **Who did** Lena **call**?

camp.text: We read Lena's travel blog, marked the verbs in colours and found the **rules** of the simple past ourselves.
camp.textDe: Wir haben Lenas Reiseblog gelesen, die Verben farbig markiert und die Regeln des simple past selbst herausgefunden.

reading.title: Lena's travel blog: My week at the Great Barrier Reef
paragraphs: Hi, I'm Lena (15) from Münster. Last summer I stayed with a host family in Cairns, Australia. Here is my best week!

On Monday we went to the reef with our guide, Mr Lee. The water looked like a postcard, and the coral was so colourful! I tried snorkelling for the first time. I jumped into the water – and then I saw a turtle. It swam right under me!

On Wednesday we took a boat to a small island. We didn't sleep in a hotel – we slept in tents on the beach. In the evening we cooked fish on a fire and watched the stars. My host brother Jack wasn't hungry, so I ate his fish too.

Mr Lee also told us a sad story. In 2016 the water was too warm, and a lot of coral died. "People didn't do enough for the reef," he said. So the next morning Jack and I collected rubbish on the beach.
On Friday the sea was rough, and the boat stopped early. I didn't feel well, and the other tourists weren't happy either.
When I got home two weeks ago, my little cousin Ben had a lot of questions:
dialog: No, I didn't. But I saw a turtle!
Were you scared in the water?
Yes, I was – but only for a minute.
What did you eat on the island?
reading.vocab: host family – Gastfamilie · coral – Koralle · turtle – Schildkröte · tent – Zelt · rubbish – Müll · rough – stürmisch · scared – ängstlich · delicious – lecker

areaLabels.Q: Verneinung, Fragen und Kurzantworten (haven't, Have you …? – Yes, I have.)
areaLabels.USE: Signalwörter: ever, never, already, just, yet

rules.title: When?
rules.text: Something happened **at some time** – the exact time is **not important**.
rules.textDe: Etwas ist irgendwann passiert, der Zeitpunkt ist egal.

rules.title: have / has + 3rd form
rules.text: he / she / it → **has** · regular: help → **helped** · irregular: see → **seen**, fly → **flown**, be → **been**
rules.textDe: Immer mit have/has – auch wenn man im Deutschen „sein“ sagt.

rules.title: Not
rules.text: **haven't / hasn't** + 3rd form
rules.textDe: haven't/hasn't + 3. Form

rules.title: Questions
rules.text: **Have / Has** + subject + 3rd form? Short answer: Yes, I **have**. / No, she **hasn't**.
rules.textDe: Frage mit Have/Has, Kurzantwort mit have/has.
rules.ex: **Have** you ever **ridden** a camel? – No, I **haven't**.

rules.title: Signal words
rules.text: **just · already · ever · never · not … yet** – yet goes at the end.
rules.textDe: Diese Wörter zeigen: present perfect! yet steht am Ende.

rules.title: since or for?
rules.text: **since** + point in time (since 1928, since Monday) · **for** + period (for two hours, for ten years)
rules.textDe: Seit wann / wie lange – im Deutschen oft Präsens!

challenge.title: Challenge: where does the signal word go?
challenge.text: just, already, ever, never → between **have/has** and the 3rd form: I have **already** finished. · **yet** → at the end: Have you finished **yet**?

camp.title: Ruby's email: we found the rules
camp.text: We read Ruby's email from the Outback, marked have/has and the 3rd forms and found the **rules** of the present perfect ourselves.
camp.textDe: Wir haben Rubys E-Mail aus dem Outback gelesen, have/has und die 3. Formen markiert und die Regeln des present perfect selbst herausgefunden.

reading.title: An email from the Outback
paragraphs: Lena met Ruby (14) at the airport in Cairns. Ruby lives on a cattle station in the Outback – and she has just sent Lena an email.

Hi Lena, how are you? Have you unpacked your suitcase yet? 😉 I have lived on Wirra Station all my life. Our nearest town is 300 kilometres away, so I have never been to a cinema! I have always done my lessons at home with the School of the Air. My teacher lives in Alice Springs – I have met her only twice.

This year has been very exciting. The Flying Doctors have visited our station three times. My little brother Sam has broken his arm twice since January – he climbs everything! And big news: Dad has just bought a small plane, and I have already flown with him four times.
It hasn't rained for six months, so everything is red and dusty. We haven't seen a kangaroo for weeks – they have all gone to the river.
Have you ever ridden a horse? I have had my horse, Biscuit, for three years. You must visit us! Write soon! – Ruby
P.S. Has Jack told you? He has found a summer job at the reef!
reading.vocab: cattle station – Rinderfarm · nearest – nächste · School of the Air – Schule per Funk und Internet · to break – brechen · dusty – staubig · to ride – reiten

SPPP.name: Simple past or present perfect?
SPPP.topic: Have you ever seen a croc?
SPPP.label: below

areaLabels.TIME: present perfect mit Zeitpunkt (yesterday, ago, last …, When …?)
areaLabels.SIGNAL: Signalwort des present perfect übersehen (ever, never, just, already, yet, since, for)
areaLabels.SPFORM: Form des simple past (-ed, unregelmäßig, did)

rules.title: Simple past: when exactly
rules.text: A **finished** action at a **time in the past**: yesterday · last week · in July · two years ago · in 2015
rules.textDe: Zu einer bestimmten Zeit passiert – auch in Erzählungen.

rules.title: Present perfect: at some time
rules.text: The time is **not important** – an experience or a result **now**: just · already · ever · never · not … yet · before
rules.textDe: Irgendwann passiert, oft mit Folgen für jetzt.
rules.ex: Oh no! I **have lost** my key.

rules.title: When …? → simple past
rules.text: Questions with **When** are always in the simple past.
rules.textDe: Fragen mit When → simple past.

rules.title: since / for → present perfect
rules.text: How long until **now**? → present perfect – even if German uses the present tense!
rules.textDe: Im Deutschen Präsens: „Ich wohne seit …“

rules.title: Talking about it
rules.text: Experience → present perfect, then the details → simple past.
rules.textDe: Erst die Erfahrung, dann die Einzelheiten.
rules.ex: **Have** you ever **seen** a croc? – Yes! I **saw** one in Darwin.

challenge.title: Challenge: German traps
challenge.text: Ich wohne **seit** 2015 hier → I **have lived** here since 2015. · Ich habe ihn **gestern** gesehen → I **saw** him yesterday. · Ich war **noch nie** dort → I **have never been** there.

reading.title: Lena's travel blog, part 2: Back home
paragraphs: Hi, it's Lena again! I have been back in Münster for two weeks now. Since then, my little cousin Ben has asked me a hundred questions. So here is our interview!
dialog: Have you ever seen a crocodile?
Yes, I have! I saw a huge one in Darwin. We went on a boat trip there in August.
Cool! Have you ever touched a shark?
No, I have never touched a shark. But last summer I swam with a turtle.
Have you shown me all your photos yet?
No, I haven't shown you the best ones yet. I have just put them on my laptop.
I came home two weeks ago. My suitcase is still in the hall – I haven't unpacked it yet!
Have you talked to Jack since then?
Yes, we have talked on the phone three times. We have been friends for six months now.
The reef! I have seen a lot of beautiful places, but that day at the reef was the best day of my life.
reading.vocab: huge – riesig · to touch – berühren · to show – zeigen · suitcase – Koffer · hall – Flur · to unpack – auspacken

areaLabels.HEAD: gute Überschrift erkennen
areaLabels.REASON: Argument mit Begründung oder Beispiel stützen

rules.title: Headline
rules.text: Short and **catchy** – it makes people want to read.
rules.textDe: Kurz und neugierig machend.

rules.title: Introduction
rules.text: **Hook** the reader (a question or a surprising fact) and say what the article is about.
rules.textDe: Leser neugierig machen und das Thema nennen.
rules.ex: **Have you ever** dreamed of swimming with turtles? … But is Australia really worth the long trip?

rules.title: Main part
rules.text: **One paragraph for each argument:** the argument + a **reason** or an **example**.
rules.textDe: Ein Absatz pro Argument: Argument + Begründung oder Beispiel.
rules.ex: Firstly, Australia has amazing wildlife. **For example**, you can see koalas in the wild.

rules.title: Linking words
rules.text: Connect your ideas: **firstly · also · in addition · however · on the other hand · for example · because · so · in conclusion**
rules.textDe: Verbinde deine Gedanken – so wird der Text flüssig.
rules.ex: The flight is long. **However**, it is worth it.

rules.title: Time phrases
rules.text: Time phrases show the **tense**: every year (simple present) · last summer, ago (simple past) · since, for, ever (present perfect)
rules.textDe: Zeitangaben zeigen dir die Zeitform.

rules.title: Conclusion
rules.text: Sum up and give **your opinion**. End with a strong last sentence.
rules.textDe: Zusammenfassen, deine Meinung, ein starker letzter Satz.
rules.ex: **In conclusion**, … **In my opinion**, … Go and see it for yourself!

intro.en: Learn what makes a good article – step by step. You need this for your own article and for the class test.
intro.de: Lerne Schritt für Schritt, was einen guten Artikel ausmacht. Das brauchst du für deinen eigenen Artikel und für die Klassenarbeit.

facts: you can do it at home, too

sections.title: What makes a good article?
sections.de: Was macht einen guten Artikel aus?

lead.en: An article is for the readers of a **magazine** or a **website**. It is not a letter – no "Dear …", no "Love, …".
lead.de: Ein Artikel ist für die Leser einer Zeitschrift oder Webseite. Er ist kein Brief.

task.en: Tap the parts in the right order: first the headline, then …
task.de: Tippe die Teile in der richtigen Reihenfolge an: zuerst die Überschrift, dann …

parts.label: Headline
parts.text: Down Under – worth the long trip?

parts.label: Introduction
parts.text: Have you ever dreamed of seeing a kangaroo in the wild? Every year, millions of tourists travel to Australia. But is it really worth visiting? Let’s take a look.

parts.label: Argument 1
parts.text: Firstly, Australia has amazing nature. You can swim at the Great Barrier Reef, the biggest coral reef in the world. For example, you can see turtles and colourful fish there.

parts.label: Argument 2
parts.text: However, there are also some problems. The flight from Germany takes more than 20 hours, and it is very expensive. That is why you should stay for at least three weeks.

parts.label: Conclusion
parts.text: In conclusion, Australia is far away, but in my opinion it is definitely worth visiting. If you get the chance, go!

items.q: Which is the best **headline**?
options: Australia: facts about the sixth biggest country in the world
Sun, sharks and 20 hours on a plane – is it worth it?
My holiday in Australia last summer
items.why: It makes you curious and shows the question of the article. The first one sounds like a fact file, the last one like a diary.
items.whyDe: Sie macht neugierig und zeigt die Frage des Artikels. Die erste klingt nach Steckbrief, die letzte nach Tagebuch.

items.q: Which is the best **headline**?
options: Australia is the best country in the world and everybody should go there
Down Under: dream trip or nightmare?
items.why: Short and catchy, and it shows there are two sides. The second one is too long and gives the answer away.
items.whyDe: Kurz, macht neugierig und zeigt zwei Seiten. Die zweite ist zu lang und verrät schon die Antwort.

items.q: Which is the best **introduction**?
options: Australia is a very big country. It has six states and two territories. The capital is Canberra, and many people live in Sydney and Melbourne.
Imagine you are snorkelling next to a turtle while it is snowing at home in Germany. Sounds great? But a trip to Australia is long and expensive. So is it really worth it?
I think Australia is definitely worth visiting because it has great beaches, amazing animals and friendly people. The weather is nice, too.
items.why: It hooks the reader with a picture in your head and then asks the question. The first one only gives facts, the last one already gives all the arguments.
items.whyDe: Sie macht mit einem Bild im Kopf neugierig und stellt dann die Frage. Die erste nennt nur Fakten, die letzte verrät schon alle Argumente.

items.q: Which is the best **introduction**?
options: Hello! My name is Tim and I am 14 years old. Today I want to tell you something about Australia.
Did you know that Australia has more than 10,000 beaches? Beaches are great. You can swim there and play volleyball with your friends.
Did you know that Australia has more than 10,000 beaches? You could visit a new one every day for 27 years! But are beaches enough to make the long trip worth it?
items.why: A surprising fact as a hook – and then the question of the article. The second one has a hook, but no question. The first one sounds like a speech, not an article.
items.whyDe: Ein überraschender Fakt als Hook – und dann die Frage. Die zweite hat einen Hook, aber keine Frage. Die erste klingt wie ein Vortrag.

task.en: All texts are about the question "Is Australia worth visiting?". Which one works best?
task.de: Alle Texte gehören zur Frage „Is Australia worth visiting?“. Was funktioniert am besten?

task.en: Which sentence supports the argument best? Careful: all of them are about Australia.
task.de: Welcher Satz stützt das Argument am besten? Vorsicht: Alle passen zum Thema Australien.

items.q: **Firstly, Australia has amazing wildlife.** …
options: Australia is a very big country with lots of different animals and plants.
For example, you can watch koalas sleeping in eucalyptus trees and see wild kangaroos in the evening.
However, some animals like snakes and spiders can be really dangerous.
items.why: It gives a concrete example. The first one only repeats the argument, the last one is a counter-argument.
items.whyDe: Er nennt ein konkretes Beispiel. Der erste wiederholt nur das Argument, der letzte ist ein Gegenargument.

items.q: **On the other hand, a trip to Australia is very expensive.** …
options: For example, a flight from Germany costs about 1,500 euros, and hotels in Sydney are expensive, too.
For example, Sydney is a very big and famous city with lots of tourists.
But it is a great experience that you will never forget.
items.why: It shows with numbers why it is expensive. The second example does not fit the argument, the last one argues against it.
items.whyDe: Er zeigt mit Zahlen, warum es teuer ist. Das zweite Beispiel passt nicht zum Argument, der letzte widerspricht ihm.

items.q: **Another good reason to go is the culture of the Aboriginal people.** …
options: Aboriginal culture is very interesting and it is also very important.
Many tourists also visit the Sydney Opera House and Bondi Beach.
Aboriginal people have lived in Australia for more than 50,000 years, so you can learn about one of the oldest cultures in the world.
items.why: It gives a fact and a reason (so …). The first one stays too general, the second one is about something else.
items.whyDe: Er nennt einen Fakt und einen Grund (so …). Der erste bleibt zu allgemein, der zweite handelt von etwas anderem.

items.q: **The weather is another argument for a visit.** …
options: The weather in Australia is different in different parts of the country.
In the north it is warm all year, so you can go swimming even at Christmas.
When my uncle was in Melbourne, it rained every day.
items.why: It explains why the weather is a reason to go. The first one is too general, the last one is an argument against.
items.whyDe: Er erklärt, warum das Wetter für eine Reise spricht. Der erste ist zu allgemein, der letzte spricht dagegen.

items.q: ___, Australia has wonderful beaches.
You can ___ see kangaroos and koalas.
Australia is beautiful. ___, it is very far away.
There are many dangerous animals, ___ snakes and spiders.
Many people go to Sydney ___ the Opera House is so famous.
The flight is very long. ___, it is expensive.
The sun is very strong, ___ you should always wear sun cream.
___, I think Australia is worth visiting.

task.en: Look at the verb. Which time phrase fits?
task.de: Schau auf das Verb. Welche Zeitangabe passt?

items.q: ___, millions of tourists visit the Great Barrier Reef.
___, my cousin travelled around Australia.
The reef has lost a lot of its coral ___.
Uluru has been a World Heritage Site ___.
The first Europeans came to Australia more than 200 years ___.
Which is the best **conclusion**?
options: In conclusion, Australia has amazing wildlife, beautiful beaches and friendly people. Also, the flight is very long.
In conclusion, I think Australia is worth visiting. Another reason is that you can go surfing at Bondi Beach.
All in all, the long flight and the high costs are a problem. But in my opinion, the wildlife, the beaches and the friendly people make Australia worth every cent. So start saving!
items.why: It sums up both sides, gives an opinion and ends strongly. The first one has no opinion, the second one brings a new argument.
items.whyDe: Er fasst beide Seiten zusammen, nennt die Meinung und endet stark. Der erste hat keine Meinung, der zweite bringt ein neues Argument.

items.q: Which is the best **conclusion**?
options: To sum up, Australia is far away, but its nature is unique. If you love animals and the sea, it is the perfect place for you – just bring a lot of sun cream!
To sum up, Australia is far away. Maybe it is worth visiting, maybe not. Everybody has to decide for themselves.
To sum up, I think Australia is worth visiting. In this article I have written about Australia. Thank you for reading.
items.why: Clear opinion and a strong, friendly last sentence. The second one has no clear opinion, the last one ends weakly.
items.whyDe: Klare Meinung und ein starker letzter Satz. Der zweite hat keine klare Meinung, der letzte endet schwach.

task.en: A good conclusion sums up, gives your opinion and has a strong last sentence – but no new arguments.
task.de: Ein guter Schluss fasst zusammen, nennt deine Meinung und hat einen starken letzten Satz – aber keine neuen Argumente.

sections.title: Your article toolkit

lead.en: Use this checklist for your own article – and in the class test.
lead.de: Nutze diese Checkliste für deinen eigenen Artikel – und in der Klassenarbeit.

checklist: an introduction with a hook and the question
eine Einleitung mit Hook und der Frage
3–4 Argumente, jedes in einem eigenen Absatz
a reason or an example for every argument
zu jedem Argument eine Begründung oder ein Beispiel
the right tenses and time phrases

done.en: And now you know how a good article works!
done.de: Jetzt weißt du, wie ein guter Artikel funktioniert!

rules.title: For and against
rules.text: First collect arguments for **both** sides.
rules.textDe: Sammle zuerst Argumente für beide Seiten.
rules.ex: for: amazing wildlife · against: the long flight

rules.title: Weigh them
rules.text: Which arguments are **most important** for your readers? Choose **3–4**.
rules.textDe: Welche Argumente sind für deine Leser am wichtigsten? Wähle 3–4 aus.
rules.ex: A koala in the wild is more exciting than six states.

rules.title: Argument + reason
rules.text: Every argument needs a **reason** or an **example**.
rules.textDe: Jedes Argument braucht eine Begründung oder ein Beispiel.
rules.ex: The flight is very expensive. **For example**, it costs about 1,500 euros.

rules.title: Strongest last
rules.text: Put your **strongest** argument at the end of the main part – right before your conclusion.
rules.textDe: Dein stärkstes Argument kommt ans Ende des Hauptteils – direkt vor den Schluss.

intro.en: Collect arguments, choose your best ones and make a plan for your article. You need your plan at Uluru.
intro.de: Sammle Argumente, wähle deine besten aus und mach einen Plan für deinen Artikel. Deinen Plan brauchst du am Uluru.

lesson.question: Is Australia worth visiting?

args.text: You can see koalas, kangaroos and wombats in the wild.
The flight from Germany takes more than 20 hours.
You can go snorkelling at the Great Barrier Reef, the biggest coral reef in the world.
Flights and hotels are very expensive.
There are more than 10,000 beaches – great for swimming and surfing.
Some animals are dangerous, for example snakes, spiders and box jellyfish.
When it is winter in Germany, it is summer in Australia.
The sun is very strong, and in summer there can be bush fires.
Australians are known as friendly and relaxed people.
The distances are huge: from Sydney to Perth it is about 4,000 km.
You can learn about Aboriginal culture, one of the oldest cultures in the world.
Because of the time difference, you feel tired for the first days (jet lag).
You can practise your English every day.
Long flights are bad for the climate.
The Outback and Uluru are an adventure you cannot have in Europe.

lead.en: The question of your article: **Is Australia worth visiting?** Before you write, you need a plan.
lead.de: Die Frage deines Artikels: Lohnt sich eine Reise nach Australien? Bevor du schreibst, brauchst du einen Plan.

task.en: Is this an argument **for** or **against** a trip to Australia?
task.de: Spricht das für oder gegen eine Reise nach Australien?

task.en: Choose **3 or 4** arguments that are most important for you. Tip: one argument against makes your article stronger.
task.de: Wähle 3 oder 4 Argumente, die dir am wichtigsten sind. Tipp: Ein Gegenargument macht deinen Artikel stärker.

sections.title: Your opinion and your reasons

task.en: What do you think? Then write a reason or an example for every argument.
task.de: Was meinst du? Dann schreib zu jedem Argument eine Begründung oder ein Beispiel.

starters: I think this is a problem because …

lead.en: This is your plan. It is saved on this iPad. At **Uluru**, it is copied together with your start code – you do not have to do anything.
lead.de: Das ist dein Plan. Er ist auf diesem iPad gespeichert. Am Uluru wird er automatisch mit deinem Startcode kopiert.

done.en: Your plan is ready – take it to Uluru!
done.de: Dein Plan ist fertig – nimm ihn mit zum Uluru!
